issues.legal_issue: The party alleging that property held by a religious head is subject to a public religious or charitable trust bears the burden of proving that character, and the holder’s failure to produce unavailable founding grants does not by itself justify an adverse inference.
material_facts: The properties had been in the possession and management of successive religious heads since the founding head acquired them.
The founding grants were not produced because they could not be traced.
The party alleging a public trust did not attempt to obtain the relevant estate records, which could have contained copies of the grants.
issues.conclusion: The burden of proving that the properties were held on trust for public religious or charitable purposes rested on the party alleging the trust. The trial court erred in drawing an adverse inference against the religious head merely because he did not produce the unavailable grants.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(1) of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951, the relevant statutory definition concerns public trusts and does not include private trusts, as held in Mahant Ramsaroop Das Ji v. S. P. Sahi, 1959 Supp. 2 S.C.R. 583. Where properties are in the religious head’s possession, the party asserting that they are held for public purposes must prove that assertion. Parmanand v. Nihal Chand, [1938] I.L.R. 65 I.A. 252, is relied on in addressing the burden and the unavailable grants.

rule.if: public_trust_status_dispute and properties_possessed_by_religious_head and claimant_alleges_public_purpose and founding_grants_unavailable and claimant_did_not_seek_available_records

predicates.public_trust_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property held by a religious institution or its head is subject to a public trust.
predicates.properties_possessed_by_religious_head: A religious head and predecessors in that office have possessed and managed the properties.
predicates.claimant_alleges_public_purpose: A claimant asserts that the properties are held for public religious or charitable purposes.
predicates.founding_grants_unavailable: The original instruments by which the founding religious head acquired the properties cannot be produced because they cannot be traced.
predicates.claimant_did_not_seek_available_records: The claimant did not attempt to obtain other records that might contain evidence of the founding grants.

issues.definition: When a claimant alleges a public trust over properties possessed by a religious head, and the founding grants are unavailable while the claimant has not sought potentially relevant records, the claimant must prove the public trust without an adverse inference based only on the missing grants.

issues.legal_issue: Celibacy among religious heads and succession from guru to chela do not, without more, raise a presumption that the properties they hold are public religious properties.
material_facts: The religious heads were celibate members of a religious order.
The office passed from guru to chela, with the reigning head selecting a successor from among his disciples.
The founding head had acquired the properties, and the later succession of the properties did not itself establish a public dedication.
issues.conclusion: Neither the celibacy of the religious heads nor succession from guru to chela raised a presumption that the properties were religious properties held for the public.
issues.legal_principle: Parmanand v. Nihal Chand, [1938] I.L.R. 65 I.A. 252, establishes that celibacy and descent of property from guru to chela do not, by themselves, show that property originally acquired by a religious head has become religious property or lost its secular character.

rule.if: public_trust_status_dispute and property_acquired_by_religious_head and religious_heads_are_celibate and succession_follows_guru_chela_line

predicates.public_trust_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property held by a religious institution or its head is subject to a public trust.
predicates.property_acquired_by_religious_head: A religious head acquired the property before it passed to successors.
predicates.religious_heads_are_celibate: The religious heads holding the property are celibate.
predicates.succession_follows_guru_chela_line: The religious office and associated property pass from a teacher to a disciple.

issues.definition: In a dispute over public-trust status, when a religious head acquired the property and celibate heads succeed through a guru-to-chela line, those features do not create a presumption of a public trust.

issues.legal_issue: Public access to a temple, festival attendance and offerings, and food or shelter provided to visitors do not, by themselves, establish that a temple or its properties are dedicated to public religious or charitable purposes.
material_facts: Members of the public visited the temple for worship and darshan without hindrance, attended festivals, and made offerings.
Sadhus, pilgrims, and other visitors were given food and shelter.
The evidence did not reliably establish that public access was exercised as a right or that the properties had been dedicated to the public.
issues.conclusion: The evidence of public access, festivals, offerings, and hospitality was not by itself sufficient to establish a public temple or a public trust over its properties.
issues.legal_principle: The evidentiary value of public use depends on circumstances supporting an inference that the use was as of right; free admission alone does not warrant readily inferring public dedication. Hospitality to sadhus and visitors may be incidental to worship and does not itself establish a public trust. The Court relied on Parmanand v. Nihal Chand, [1938] I.L.R. 65 I.A. 252; Ramsaran Das v. Jai Ram Das, A.I.R. 1943 Pat. 135; and Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop, 67 I.A. 1.

rule.if: public_trust_status_dispute and public_visitors_enter_without_obstruction and visitors_receive_food_or_shelter and festivals_or_offerings_occur and no_reliable_evidence_of_use_as_of_right

predicates.public_trust_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property held by a religious institution or its head is subject to a public trust.
predicates.public_visitors_enter_without_obstructio: Members of the public visit a temple without being obstructed.
predicates.visitors_receive_food_or_shelter: Sadhus, pilgrims, or other visitors are provided with food or shelter.
predicates.festivals_or_offerings_occur: Festivals are held with public attendance or visitors make offerings at the institution.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_use_as_of_right: The evidence does not reliably show that the public used the institution as of right.

issues.definition: When public visitors enter without obstruction, receive hospitality, and attend festivals or make offerings, those facts alone do not establish public dedication if reliable evidence that their use was as of right is absent.

issues.legal_issue: A mutt may be either private or public, and its character depends on whether the endowment benefits the public or an unascertained class, rather than only the grantee or an ascertained group, assessed from the grant and the institution’s established circumstances.
material_facts: The institution was a religious asthal with a temple and properties managed by its head.
The evidence included the manner in which properties were acquired, managed, and dealt with, and the institution’s practices and use.
The evidence did not establish that the institution’s endowment was intended to benefit the public or an unascertained class.
issues.conclusion: The Court recognized that a mutt can be private or public and that its character must be determined from the grant or the circumstances, including usage, custom, and the manner in which its properties have been dealt with.
issues.legal_principle: A mutt dedicated for ascetics generally or for the ascetics of a particular sect may be public, while an endowment intended to maintain a particular spiritual family or benefit the grantee or an ascertained group may be private. The court must determine the endowment’s beneficiaries from the grant and the established circumstances, including usage, custom, and dealings with the properties. The Court referred to Matam Nadipudi v. Board of Commissioners for Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras, A.I.R. 1938 Mad. 810, and Missir v. Das, [1949] I.L.R. 28 Pat. 890.

predicates.mutt_public_or_private_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a religious mutt or asthal is a public or private institution.
predicates.evidence_about_grant_or_institutional_ci: Evidence is available about the grant, the institution’s usage or custom, or the way its properties have been managed and dealt with.

issues.definition: In a dispute over whether a mutt is public or private, its character depends on the intended beneficiaries as assessed from the grant and the institution’s established circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: Permanent installation of deities, the physical arrangement of temple and residential premises, and descriptions of properties as appertaining to an asthal do not, without more, establish that the properties are subject to a public trust.
material_facts: The deities were installed permanently on a pedestal, and the temple was said to stand on grounds separate from the religious head’s residential quarters, although evidence showed that the quarters were not in fact separate from the temple premises.
Successor-appointment documents described properties as appertaining to the asthal.
There was no independent proof establishing that the asthal itself was dedicated as a public trust.
issues.conclusion: The physical features and the description of properties as appertaining to the asthal did not establish a public dedication or public trust.
issues.legal_principle: Permanent installation and the physical arrangement of temple premises are not conclusive because similar features occur in private temples and mutts. The phrase “appertaining to the asthal” indicates, at most, that properties form part of the asthal; it does not make them public-trust properties unless the asthal itself is a public trust. The Court relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, [1956] S.C.R. 756 at 761, and Sri Thakurji Ramji v. Mathura Prasad, A.I.R. 1941 Pat. 354 at 358.

predicates.public_trust_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property held by a religious institution or its head is subject to a public trust.
predicates.permanent_deity_installation_or_temple_l: Deities are permanently installed or the temple has a physical arrangement said to indicate public dedication.
predicates.documents_call_properties_appertaining_t: Documents describe properties as appertaining to or forming part of a mutt or asthal.
predicates.no_independent_proof_mutt_is_public: There is no independent evidence establishing that the mutt or asthal itself is a public institution.

issues.definition: When physical features and document descriptions are present but there is no independent proof that the mutt is public, those features and descriptions alone do not establish a public trust.

issues.legal_issue: Properties managed and held by successive religious heads were not shown to be public-trust properties where the evidence did not establish a public dedication or public use as of right.
material_facts: The properties were recorded in the names of the religious heads, who possessed and managed them throughout.
Successors were selected by the reigning head from among his disciples, without public participation.
The religious heads acquired additional properties in their own names and dealt with properties by sale, mortgage, and lease without objection.
The evidence of public access, hospitality, and other religious activities did not reliably establish a public dedication or public use as of right.
issues.conclusion: The party alleging a public trust failed to establish that the properties fell within the Act’s definition of a religious trust. The Act therefore did not apply to the properties, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1) of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951, covered public religious or charitable trusts and excluded private trusts, as explained in Mahant Ramsaroop Das Ji v. S. P. Sahi, 1959 Supp. 2 S.C.R. 583. The Court assessed the grant and surrounding circumstances, including possession, management, property dealings, institutional practice, and the evidence of public use, applying the principles in Parmanand v. Nihal Chand, [1938] I.L.R. 65 I.A. 252, and Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop, 67 I.A. 1.

rule.if: appeal_over_public_trust_classification and properties_recorded_in_religious_heads_names and religious_heads_controlled_property_and_successor_selection and property_dealings_were_unobjected_to and no_reliable_evidence_of_public_dedication

predicates.appeal_over_public_trust_classification: An appeal concerns whether property of a religious institution is held under a public trust.
predicates.properties_recorded_in_religious_heads_n: The properties are recorded in the names of the religious heads rather than in the name of a deity or institution.
predicates.religious_heads_controlled_property_and_: Religious heads possessed and managed the property and selected their successors without public participation.
predicates.property_dealings_were_unobjected_to: Religious heads dealt with the properties, including through transfers or encumbrances, without objection.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_public_dedicatio: Reliable evidence does not establish that the properties were dedicated to public religious or charitable purposes.

issues.definition: On an appeal over public-trust classification, where religious heads held and controlled the properties and selected successors, their dealings were unobjected to, and reliable evidence of public dedication is absent, the properties are not established as public-trust property and the statutory regime does not apply.
